source.title: Unsupervised discovery of functional sequence patterns from protein language model with MotifAE
source.authors: Chao Hou; Di Liu; Yu-Feng Shen

record.file_problem: none noted; full article text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates learned sparse-autoencoder features in a protein language model, not the model's own neurons or the claim versions' neuron-explanation tests.
record.gate_note: The paper calls sparse-autoencoder latent units features and studies their matches to protein motifs and domains. These are not measurements of how many native model neurons have one or more jobs, or tests of explanations on activations not used to write them. Relevant feature results are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study trains a sparse autoencoder with a smoothness loss on ESM2-650M last-layer embeddings. It evaluates the SAE latent features against protein motifs, domains and mutation data. It never measures how many of ESM2's native neurons have one main job. It has no Qwen3-32B audit, cross-model neuron shares, InceptionV1 analysis, attribution graphs, or held-out simulation scoring of neuron explanations. It adopts the SAE premise that embeddings are linear combinations of more features than dimensions. That is the superposition framing the claim disputes, but the study does not test it against native neurons. The claim's original sources are not cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the smoothness loss helps the SAE recover coherent sequence patterns, including known motifs and some domains. Feature activations track residue importance, features vary in granularity, and supervised gating finds stability-associated features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an SAE on ESM2 protein embeddings with a sequence smoothness loss and evaluates learned features against biological annotations; it does not use the original neuron-pole audit or test neuron explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: MotifAE with smoothness loss outperformed standard SAE on motif and domain identification; the authors report similar performance for smoothness window sizes of three, four, and five residues.

fits_no_version.finding: Of 114 matched ELM motifs, 47 are matched by one MotifAE feature and 67 by several (AUROC>0.9). Of 146 matched features, 91 match one motif and 55 match several. Feature f27416 covers 17 C-terminal motifs and has no predictive power for non-C-terminal motifs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features of a protein language model vary in functional granularity: some map to a single annotated motif, others to a shared general function.

fits_no_version.finding: 6,421 of 40,960 MotifAE features show coherent 5–30 residue activations across 2.3M proteins.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Only a minority of learned protein-LM SAE features show coherent, motif-like sequence activations.

record.problems: The results concern learned SAE features in a protein language model, not native model neurons. Motif and domain matching does not directly measure whether a feature has one named job, and the study does not test explanations on activations withheld from explanation-writing.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles; no one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
No native-neuron job shares in any language model, dense or MoE, at any scale; ESM2 native neurons are not analysed.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron re-analysis.
No interpretable native-neuron shares across architectures or tools. The SAE versus MotifAE comparison concerns learned dictionaries, not native neurons.
No attribution graphs or neuron-based circuit explanations compared to replacement models.
No test of activating-example explanations against where native neurons fire.
No simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'assumes': the paper never discusses neuron cleanliness but builds on the SAE linear-superposition premise. The Discussion cites Simon et al., who found SAEs more interpretable than raw pLM embedding neurons. That is a cited result, not this study's own, and is relevant context against V2 for protein models only if read in the original. All rows are correctly linked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimates of the one-job, two-job, or unexplained shares.
No comparison of neuron-job shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or model scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No estimates of interpretable native-neuron shares in vision models or tests of architecture, regularization, and tool effects on those shares.
No attribution graphs or comparison of neuron-based explanations with replacement models.
No test of explanations written from activating examples against where neurons fire.
No automated neuron-explanation scoring on new text.

relation.reason: The study does not assume native neurons are clean. It treats pLMs as black boxes and takes the SAE premise (embeddings are linear combinations of features). It only cites Simon et al.'s result that SAE latents beat raw pLM embeddings on interpretability, to justify leaving out that control. It does not cite the claim's sources or discuss them. 'Assumes' would wrongly suggest it relies on the finding.

tranche.reason: Trains an SAE with a smoothness loss on ESM2-650M last-layer embeddings and scores the learned latents against ELM motifs, CATH domains and DMS data. It never measures native ESM2 neurons and neither tests nor uses the claim.

source_check.notes: All rows concern learned MotifAE (SAE) latents on ESM2-650M (window size 3 in main figures), not native neurons. No version is tested and no verdicts are recorded, which is right. The only bearing on raw-neuron interpretability is a cited result (Simon et al., InterPLM); the study runs no raw-neuron control itself.
